title: aki vs. amely: People and Things

sections.content: This lesson is about a document, the Golden Bull, so you need a relative pronoun for things as well as people. Hungarian keeps these strictly separate: 'aki' only ever refers to a person, while 'amely' (and its plural 'amelyek') refers back to a thing, a document, an institution or any other non-person noun that was already named. A closely related word, 'ami', is used instead of 'amely' when there's no specific earlier noun to point back to (roughly 'what' or 'whatever') — 'amely' is the one you'll need most for referring to something specific, like a named law.

sections.title: Choosing the right relative pronoun
rows: which, that (a specific thing already named — a law, a document, an institution)
what, that (general or indefinite reference, no specific antecedent)

items.spanish: II. András, aki 1222-ben kiadta az Aranybullát, engedett a nemesség nyomásának.
items.english: Andrew II, who issued the Golden Bull in 1222, gave in to the nobility's pressure.

items.spanish: Az Aranybulla, amely korlátozta a király hatalmát, sok tekintetben az angol Magna Chartához hasonlít.
items.english: The Golden Bull, which limited the king's power, resembles England's Magna Carta in many ways.

items.spanish: A törvény, amelyet a nemesek kikényszerítettek, biztosította az ellenállás jogát.
items.english: The law that the nobles forced through guaranteed the right of resistance.

sections.content: A common mistake at this level is using 'aki' for a document or institution, on the model of English 'the law who...'. Always ask first: is the antecedent a person, or a thing? 'II. András' is a person → 'aki'. 'Az Aranybulla' is a document → 'amely'. Once you have the two pronouns straight, you can describe a whole event in one sentence: who did it (aki), and what it produced (amely).
